Auzaar: the night before the guarantees

Sunday, 7 February 2027, Pune. In seven days Auzaar must either serve notice on 900 supply contracts or renew them for another year, and the number that would settle the argument changed its definition in September without anyone deciding that it had.

1. Sunday night

Devyani Kulkarni had been at the Baner office since two in the afternoon, which was a poor sign on a Sunday in February, and by nine she had stopped pretending the board pre-read would improve. The chief product officer of Auzaar had three documents open. The first was the finance model that showed the company ₹19.6 crore better off next year if it let its guaranteed-supply contracts lapse. The second was the supply team's model, which used the same starting numbers and arrived at ₹3 crore. The third was a message from Nikhil Basu in Toronto, sent at 11:14 a.m. his time, which read: “Before tomorrow — you should know the machine-day series is not one series. We changed the source in September. Nobody restated the earlier months. The step-up everyone keeps pointing at is mostly the change.”

The board met at eleven the next morning, Pune time, with two directors joining from Singapore and one from New Jersey. The contracts carried a forty-five day notice period against a 31 March auto-renewal, which meant that whatever the board concluded had to become a letter to 900 fleet owners by Sunday 14 February. Devyani's problem was not that she lacked a recommendation. It was that every version of her recommendation rested on a comparison between this quarter and last, and she had just been told that the two quarters were measured with different instruments.

2. How Auzaar got here

Auzaar was founded in Pune in 2021 by Suresh Patwardhan, who had spent eleven years selling construction equipment for a dealer network in Maharashtra and had watched the same backhoe sit idle in a yard in Chakan for five weeks while a contractor in Ahmednagar hired one from two hundred kilometres away. The product was a rental marketplace: a contractor posts a requisition — a 20-tonne excavator with operator, Nagpur site, eleven days from the 14th — and an owner accepts it. Auzaar handles the digital rental agreement, the GST-compliant invoice and e-way bill, escrow of the advance through a licensed payment aggregator, and a dispute process for damage and downtime. Machines are JCB, Tata Hitachi, Mahindra and Ashok Leyland; the customers are the second and third tier of the construction economy, the subcontractors who actually execute for the L&Ts and the NHAI packages.

In 2023 Auzaar made the decision that constrains everything today. Growth had stalled because contractors could not rely on getting a machine: the platform would find one on four requisitions out of ten, which is worse than useless in a business where a stalled site costs a lakh a day. So Auzaar signed guarantee contracts with 900 mid-sized fleet owners across nine clusters. In exchange for platform exclusivity and a 22 per cent commission — well above the 12 per cent it charged everyone else — Auzaar guaranteed each machine a minimum ₹1.1 lakh of monthly billing, paying the shortfall in cash if the platform failed to deliver work. Fill rate went from 41 per cent to 58 in five quarters. The company raised at a valuation that assumed it would keep going.

The guarantees also created a machine that eats. In January 2027 Auzaar paid ₹1.63 crore in shortfall payments — cash to owners for work it had not been able to find them — against ₹4.44 crore of net revenue in the same month. The contracts renew annually on 31 March. They have renewed three times.

3. The industry around it

Indian construction-equipment rental is large, fragmented and cyclical. National highway and Gati Shakti packages set the rhythm of demand; monsoon stops earthworks across most of the country between June and September; and the machines themselves come from a handful of OEM and dealer networks whose own rental arms are both partner and competitor. Auzaar's clusters straddle two quite different economies: infrastructure and mining work around Nagpur, Raipur and Hyderabad, where machines are scarce and day rates are high; and the farm-equipment corridor around Ludhiana and Bathinda, where tractors and harvesters are abundant, day rates are a third of the infrastructure rate, and demand exists for eleven weeks of the year.

Regulation shapes the product more than most people expect. Every rental generates an e-invoice and, for machine movement, an e-way bill; advances sit in escrow under the payment-aggregator framework; operator identity and location data flow through the telematics devices, which brings the DPDP Act's consent requirements into what looks like a logistics feature. And since 2026 a new pressure has arrived from outside India: Gulf contractors executing UAE and Saudi packages have begun sourcing Indian machines and Indian operators, which is how Dareen Contracting LLC, a Dubai civil contractor, came to be Auzaar's largest single prospective account and also its most complicated one.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence matters. In April 2026, under pressure from the shortfall payments, Auzaar opened the platform to non-exclusive “open supply” at 12 per cent commission and no guarantee. Open machines grew from 410 in April to 860 by December. At the same time Nikhil built the Marketplace Health Index, Exhibit 1, which combined fill rate, utilisation, dispute rate and repeat rate into a single 0–100 score with weights chosen so that the index tracked machine-days well over the preceding two quarters. The index went on the board deck and on the office wall. It has risen from 58 to 71 since April.

In July, Auzaar onboarded a 210-machine dealer network in Pune in a single month — a one-time event that dominates the open-supply growth curve that the CFO's model now extrapolates. In September, the data team switched the definition of a machine-day from operator timesheets to telematics-derived engine hours, converted at 7.5 engine-hours to the day, because timesheets were being filed late and inconsistently. The change was made in a ticket titled “fix machine-day pipeline”. Earlier months were not restated. Machine-days jumped 12 per cent in September and everyone in the company attributed it to the post-monsoon season and to open supply.

In November, shortfall payments crossed ₹1.5 crore for the first time. In December, the payment run to fleet owners was delayed by nine days because of a banking change at the payment aggregator. In the week after that delay, Ayesha Khan's team fielded the owner survey that now underpins the supply-side churn forecast in Exhibit 4. In January, Devyani learned from a sales colleague in Nagpur that at least 130 of the 900 exclusive owners were quietly listing machines on a rival platform in violation of their contracts, and that nobody in supply ops had escalated it because the owners in question were current on their utilisation and therefore invisible on every dashboard the company had.

5. The people

Devyani Kulkarni, chief product officer, Pune. Joined from a payments company nineteen months ago. Position: the company cannot decide the guarantee question until it can state, in arithmetic, what the guarantees buy. Incentive: her next two quarters of roadmap depend on which supply model survives. Not saying: she agreed in October that the machine-day pipeline change was “a data fix, not a metric change”, and signed the ticket.

Suresh Patwardhan, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: renew the guarantees at a reduced level and raise open-supply commission to 15 per cent; stability matters more than optimality this year. Incentive: a strategic investor — an equipment finance NBFC — has indicated a term sheet contingent on net revenue crossing ₹60 crore annualised. Not saying: the indication is verbal and the NBFC has asked for the shortfall liability to be quantified as a contingent obligation.

Girish Shetye, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Position: serve notice; the guarantees are a subsidy the company can no longer afford, and open supply has proved it can grow. Incentive: he has committed the board to positive contribution by Q3 FY28. Not saying: his open-supply ramp assumes July's dealer-network onboarding repeats twice more, and he has not modelled fill rate falling at all.

Ayesha Khan, head of supply network, Nagpur. Position: renewal, unchanged; the exclusive fleet is the only reason Nagpur, Raipur and Hyderabad clear at all. Incentive: her variable pay is tied to exclusive-fleet retention. Not saying: she has known about the 130 owners listing elsewhere since November and has been handling it relationship by relationship rather than reporting it.

Nikhil Basu, lead data scientist, Toronto. Position: no decision of this size should be taken on the current series; give him three weeks to restate. Incentive: he built the index and does not want it discredited by someone else first. Not saying: the restatement is not a three-week job, because timesheets for 31 per cent of machines were never filed at all.

Tanvi Raghavan, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: the Dubai opportunity changes the strategic question entirely and should be decided first. Incentive: her mandate expands if international becomes a line of business. Not saying: Dareen Contracting's procurement head has told her the volume is subject to a client approval that has not come, and she has not shared this with finance.

Rohan Bakshi, head of global accounts, Edison, New Jersey. Position: the real business is the telematics data — utilisation benchmarks sold to OEMs and insurers in North America, ₹6.2 crore of annual contract value signed in ten months at close to no marginal cost. Incentive: his quota is entirely data ARR. Not saying: device coverage on active machines has fallen from 81 per cent to 69 per cent because open-supply machines mostly arrive without devices, which is the same fact that makes the machine-day series unreliable.

Mira Falkenrath, design lead, Berlin. Position: the requisition-and-bid flow is the problem; contractors abandon it, and the fill rate everyone argues about is measured only on requisitions that were completed. Incentive: she has wanted to rebuild the flow for a year. Not saying: she has a standing offer from another company and has told only Devyani.

7. Voices

“I am not asking the board to choose between my model and Ayesha's. I am asking them to notice that the difference between them is ₹19 crore and that both were built in a week on the same spreadsheet template. If the answer is that sensitive to an assumption nobody owns, the assumption is the deliverable, not the model.”

— Devyani Kulkarni, board pre-read note, 6 February 2027

“Health index at 71, highest ever. Fill rate stable. Open supply compounding. I genuinely do not understand what we are debating.”

— Girish Shetye, in the #leadership channel, 4 February, 9:12 IST

“Girish — the index is 40 per cent fill rate and 30 per cent utilisation. If we let guaranteed machines go, fill falls and utilisation on what is left rises. The index barely moves. It was never built to survive this decision. That is my fault, not yours.”

— Nikhil Basu, same channel, 4 February, 23:41 IST (13:11 Toronto)

“Madam, machine is standing since 19 January. Last month the payment came late by nine days and I had to pay the driver from my pocket. I am not leaving Auzaar. But my brother has put two machines on the other app and he is getting work in Raipur. You tell me what to do.”

— Voice note from a guaranteed fleet owner, Bhilai, forwarded by Ayesha Khan to Devyani, 30 January 2027

“Please note our benchmark contracts renew in April and the buyers have started asking how the sample is constructed. I have been answering at a high level. I would prefer we agree what we say before somebody asks a precise question.”

— Rohan Bakshi, email to Devyani and Girish, 2 February, 21:38 EST

“Thirty-one per cent of requisitions are abandoned before submission. They are not in the fill rate, because the fill rate is calculated on submitted requisitions. Every conversation in this company is about supply and the demand side is quietly leaving the form.”

— Mira Falkenrath, design review, Berlin, 28 January 2027

8. The options as Devyani sees them

Option one: renew, at a lower guarantee. Serve no notice; renegotiate the minimum from ₹1.1 lakh to ₹85,000 per machine-month and raise open-supply commission from 12 to 15 per cent. This preserves Nagpur, Raipur and Hyderabad, keeps device coverage where it is, and protects the data business. It costs perhaps ₹13 crore of shortfall next year instead of ₹19.6, and it accepts that Auzaar is a managed fleet business wearing a marketplace's clothes. Suresh prefers it. It also requires 900 renegotiations in five weeks with owners who have just been paid late.

Option two: serve notice and go open. Let all 900 lapse on 31 March, redeploy the shortfall money — ₹19.6 crore — into matching, quality and open-supply onboarding, and accept a worse fill rate for two quarters. Girish prefers it. If Ayesha's churn estimate is right, the two starved clusters go from 49 and 55 per cent fill to somewhere neither model can predict, in the clusters that carry the highest day rates.

Option three: segment the guarantee. Renew only in the clusters where exclusive utilisation is above 70 per cent — Nagpur–Raipur and Hyderabad–Vijayawada, roughly 480 machines — and let the rest lapse, including the entire farm corridor where exclusive utilisation is 41 per cent and the company pays shortfall on machines nobody wants for nine months of the year. It is the option that survives both models in Exhibit 4, and it is the option that requires Auzaar to tell 420 owners in Punjab and NCR that their contract is ending, in writing, by 14 February.

All three options are decisions about supply. Mira's number — 31 per cent of requisitions abandoned before submission — is not in any of them, and neither is the question of whether machine-days, as currently produced, can support a comparison across September. Nor does any option address Rohan's April renewals, which depend on a device fleet concentrated precisely on the machines that options two and three release. Tanvi has argued, in writing, that the Dubai project makes the guaranteed fleet more valuable rather than less, since those are the only machines Auzaar can commit; she has not said what happens if the approval does not come.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The notice period is forty-five days against a 31 March renewal: a letter must go out by Sunday 14 February or the contracts renew for another year on existing terms. Auzaar holds ₹62 crore of cash and is burning ₹2.1 crore a month; the shortfall obligation runs at ₹1.5–1.6 crore a month and is not capped. The supply operations team is forty people across nine cities and there is a hiring freeze. The exclusivity clause in the guarantee contract is enforceable in principle and has never been enforced; enforcing it against the 130 owners now listed elsewhere would take the company into a dispute with the very fleet it needs in February. The data contracts renew in April and carry a representation about sample construction. Deploying guaranteed machines to Dubai would require an amendment to every one of those contracts, operator visas, and a customs arrangement Auzaar has never executed. And the NBFC's interest, which Suresh has not formally disclosed to the board, is contingent on a revenue run-rate that Option two does not reach in FY28 under either model in Exhibit 4.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Reconstruct Auzaar's January machine-days from the demand side and from the supply side using Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3. Where do the two reconstructions fail to meet, and what would have to be true for them to meet?

2. The Marketplace Health Index has risen from 58 to 71 while shortfall payments have risen 35 per cent. Explain, in terms of what the index is made of, how both can be true at once.

3. Exhibit 2's machine-day series changes source in September and is grossed up from a device fleet whose coverage is falling (Exhibit 5). Which conclusions in the case survive if the series is unusable before September? Which do not?

4. Girish and Ayesha (Exhibit 4) differ by ₹19 crore of contribution. Identify the three assumptions that drive the gap and design the cheapest test that would move either of them before 14 February.

5. Mira says 31 per cent of requisitions are abandoned before submission and therefore never enter the fill rate. If she is right, how does that change which side of this marketplace is actually constrained — and does it change the guarantee decision, or only the story told about it?

6. It is Monday morning, 8 February. What does Devyani do, in what order, and what exactly does she say to the board about the ₹19.6 crore, the September step-change and the letter that must go out on the 14th?

11. Sunday, 11:40 p.m.

Devyani wrote three versions of the first slide and deleted all of them. The first said the company should segment the guarantees by cluster, which was the answer that survived both models and which would require a letter to 420 owners in six days. The second said the company should renew for one more year and spend that year building a measurement system it could actually decide on, which was honest and which Girish would call an expensive way to avoid a decision, because it was one. The third said nothing about the guarantees at all and opened with Mira's 31 per cent, which was either the most important number in the company or a design lead's hobbyhorse, and Devyani could not tell which, because the only way to find out was to instrument a part of the funnel that nobody had ever measured.

Her phone showed a message from Nikhil, sent an hour earlier: “I can restate August backwards if you accept a 9% error band. I cannot restate July. Tell me whether a 9% band is useful or whether it just gives everyone a new thing to argue about.” Below it, a note from Tanvi in Singapore, timestamped 2:05 a.m. her time, saying that Dareen's procurement head had gone quiet since Thursday. Below that, nothing from Suresh, who had said at Friday's standup that he trusted her to bring one recommendation, not three.

Outside, the traffic on the Mumbai–Bengaluru highway had thinned to the sound of trucks. Devyani opened a blank document and typed, at the top, the only sentence she was sure of: “We have two customers and one number, and the number is not measured the same way it was in August.” Then she sat and looked at it for a long time.

Metric Trees for Two-Sided Products

How do you measure a marketplace without letting one side's number be bought at the other side's expense? The answer is a tree with two roots, joined at a node neither side can move alone.

1. A Monday deadline in Gurugram

On the morning of 14 July 2026, Meher Anand, VP of Growth at Tarazu Bazaar, a wholesale marketplace connecting small FMCG manufacturers with neighbourhood kirana retailers, had four days to decide what she would recommend to the board. June's numbers were respectable but not exciting: GMV, gross merchandise value — the total value of goods transacted through the platform — had reached ₹186 crore, generated by 42,000 active retailer-buyers placing an average of 3.4 orders each at an average order value of ₹1,30,000. The board had set a target of 25% quarter-on-quarter GMV growth by September, and Meher's supply-side lead had come to her with a plan that looked, on a slide, unambiguously good: pay each of Tarazu's 3,100 active wholesale sellers ₹500 for every new product listing they added. More listings, more selection, more orders, more GMV. The plan would cost roughly ₹11 crore over the quarter, comfortably inside the approved budget.

Meher had seen this movie before: a similar listings incentive at a previous employer had driven a supply dashboard from green to spectacular while the number that actually mattered — orders buyers completed — barely moved. What she needed before Monday was a way to show the board, in one picture and a few lines of arithmetic, whether growing the supply side would grow the marketplace, or merely grow a number that looked like it.

2. The idea: a tree with two roots

A metric tree, or driver tree, is a diagram that decomposes one top-line number into the smaller, more controllable numbers that multiply or add up to produce it, with each node given an owner, a review cadence, and a decision it informs. The ancestor of the form is the DuPont formula, developed inside General Motors and DuPont in the 1920s to break return on equity into profit margin, asset turnover and financial leverage. Product and growth teams adapted the idea decades later — most visibly through Dave McClure's 2007 AARRR framework (acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue) — to decompose a single population's behaviour: one group of users, one funnel, one root.

A two-sided product breaks that single-root assumption. A marketplace, a hiring platform or a payments network has two distinct populations — supply and demand — whose individual health can rise while the thing that actually creates value between them falls. Tarazu Bazaar can have record numbers of sellers and still have a marketplace that doesn't work, if those sellers' listings never meet a buyer who wants them. The metric-tree adaptation, sharpened into common use by writings such as Bill Gurley's 2011 essay on marketplace liquidity and the marketplace-investing practice at firms like a16z and NfX through the mid-2010s, is to build two roots — supply and demand — and force them to converge at a single node measuring the interaction between them, before either branch rolls up into revenue. That convergence node is usually called liquidity, or match rate: the share of one side's intent that finds a completed transaction with the other side.

The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "A marketplace's north star has to be a number that can only go up when both sides get healthier together — never when one side's count is inflated at the other's expense."

3. How it actually works

Building a two-rooted tree is a sequence of decisions, and the ones practitioners skip are usually the last two.

Start with the true north star, but treat it as an output, not a dial. For Tarazu Bazaar that is GMV. Managing this number directly is a mistake — it is the sum of everything below it, and nothing at this level tells you what to change on Tuesday.

Build the demand root. Active buyers, times orders per buyer, times average order value, each owned separately: acquisition for buyer count, lifecycle for order frequency, merchandising for order value.

Build the supply root separately, not as a mirror of the demand root. Active sellers, times listings per seller, times the fraction of those listings that are actually sellable — priced competitively, in stock, meeting quality bar. Supply health is seller count multiplied by how much of what they offer is genuinely wanted, not seller count alone.

Force the two roots to meet at one convergence node before they become GMV. Teams skip this because it is more comfortable to report two healthy branches separately than the one number that is honest about whether they met. For Tarazu, that node is match rate: completed orders divided by buyer search sessions.

Attach take rate as a guardrail, not free money. Take rate — marketplace revenue divided by GMV — sits below GMV in the tree, but a rising take rate has a delayed, negative edge back into the supply root, because sellers with alternatives respond to lower margin by listing less or leaving. A tree that shows take rate without seller retention by cohort is showing half the picture.

Assign an owner, a cadence and a decision to every node — not just the top one. If nobody's weekly review includes match rate specifically, the tree is a poster, not a management tool.

4. The worked example: what the ₹500 listing bonus actually buys

Start from June's baseline, already on the diagram above: 42,000 buyers × 3.4 orders × ₹1,30,000 average order value gives GMV of ₹185.64 crore, rounded to ₹186 crore. Revenue at a 4.2% take rate is ₹7.79 crore. On the supply side, 3,100 sellers × 240 listings gives 744,000 total listings; against 142,800 monthly orders that is a sell-through rate of 19.2%. Search sessions run at 610,000 a month, so match rate — orders divided by searches — is 23.4%.

Now run the supply lead's proposal forward. Paying ₹500 per new listing, sellers respond exactly as incentives predict: listings per seller rise from 240 to 310, a 29% jump, taking total listings to 3,100 × 310 = 961,000. But nothing in this plan touches the demand root. Buyers do not search more because there is more inventory sitting unseen in a catalogue; search sessions might tick up slightly to, say, 650,000 as new listings get indexed, but orders stay essentially flat at 142,800, because buyer intent hasn't changed. Recompute: sell-through rate falls to 142,800 / 961,000 = 14.9%, and match rate falls slightly too, to 142,800 / 650,000 = 22.0%. GMV does not move. The bonus cost, on the 217,000 new listings, is 217,000 × ₹500 = ₹10.85 crore — more than the entire month's revenue — spent to make the supply-side dashboard look better while the tree's actual convergence node got slightly worse.

Meher's second pass changes one input: instead of paying for listings, pay sellers a ₹150 completion bonus per fulfilled order — a cost tied to an actual match, not a promise of one — and spend the rest of the budget fixing search ranking so buyers find relevant stock faster. Assume this raises match rate from 23.4% to 27%, with search sessions unchanged at 610,000. Orders become 610,000 × 0.27 = 164,700, up 15.3% on baseline. GMV becomes 164,700 × ₹1,30,000 = ₹214.11 crore, up 15.3% on baseline. At the same 4.2% take rate, revenue is ₹8.99 crore, up 15.4%. The completion bonus costs 164,700 × ₹150 = ₹2.47 crore — less than a quarter of the listings plan's spend — because it only pays out when the tree's real bottleneck, the match, actually clears.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Liquidity is a rate, not a count. Match rate can rise while absolute orders fall, if searches fall faster — a shrinking, highly-satisfied marketplace looks identical on this node to a healthy one. Always read the rate beside its denominator.

Take rate is a guardrail, not a growth lever. Raising it doesn't create marketplace value; it redistributes value already created, and can quietly starve the supply root over a quarter or two before the effect shows up in GMV.

Two-sided doesn't mean symmetric. A reciprocal marketplace like a hiring platform needs a match rate defined from both directions; a one-directional fulfilment marketplace like Tarazu Bazaar only needs demand to clear against supply, and building a reciprocal metric there is wasted complexity.

The tree tells you what moved, not why. A falling match rate has many possible causes — bad ranking, thin stock in a growing city, a pricing war — and the tree cannot distinguish between them without an experiment or a cohort cut underneath it.

Averages hide a side gaming its number regionally. A national match rate can sit flat while Bengaluru thrives and Indore quietly collapses, because one city carries the average. Any two-sided tree needs its convergence node cut by geography or category before anyone trusts it.

Not every supply number is a real supply number. Listings are cheap to inflate; sellable, competitively priced, in-stock listings are not. Confusing the two is the most common way a supply root gets gamed.

The two roots move on different clocks. Demand can shift within a day of a marketing push; a supply root built on wholesaler trust takes weeks. Reviewing both on the same weekly cadence quietly pressures the supply team to fake short-term movement.

What the tree cannot tell you. It cannot set the right take rate — a competitive judgment about how much margin sellers will tolerate before switching channels — and it cannot, by itself, prove causality. It only tells you where to point an experiment next.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

At a consumer services marketplace like Saral Seva, which matches households with home-repair professionals, the demand root usually dominates: professionals are relatively elastic supply, and the convergence metric that matters most is how quickly a request gets served, often measured in hours rather than as a monthly rate. At Tarazu Bazaar the supply root dominates instead: onboarding a wholesaler involves trust, credit terms and catalogue setup that take weeks, while a retailer, once trained on the app, orders repeatedly with little further persuasion. A single-population consumer product — a news app, a fitness tracker — never needs two roots at all; forcing one onto it adds complexity nobody asked for.

Stage matters as much as category. An early marketplace is often deliberately, correctly, unbalanced: Tarazu Bazaar's founders spent its first eighteen months subsidising sellers to build a supply root thick enough that buyers would have something worth searching for. That is legitimate, but only if the tree labels the subsidy as a subsidy, with an end date, rather than letting a bought supply number masquerade as organic health. At scale, the tree's centre of gravity shifts toward the take-rate guardrail, because liquidity is established and the platform can extract margin — but the ceiling on that extraction is disintermediation risk: buyers and sellers who have met once quietly moving off-platform, a leakage the tree should track as its own named metric rather than folding into churn.

7. Common mistakes

Treating supply presence as the north star. Symptom: a dashboard proudly showing record active sellers while GMV is flat for two quarters running. The error is conflating a side's presence with its health. The cheap diagnostic: plot sell-through rate next to seller count — if one climbs while the other falls, the growth is hollow.

A convergence node with no owner. Symptom: match rate sits on a shared slide, but when it drops five points in a week, supply blames marketing and marketing blames stock quality, and nobody investigates. The diagnostic question is blunt: who gets paged when this number moves? If nobody, the tree is decoration.

Raising take rate without watching seller cohorts. Symptom: revenue jumps the quarter a rate change lands, then GMV growth quietly decelerates two quarters later. The misunderstanding is treating take rate as a free lever rather than a price elastic sellers respond to. The diagnostic is a seller-retention curve, segmented for sellers with alternative channels, run before and after the change.

Importing a single-root consumer funnel wholesale. Symptom: an acquisition-activation-retention dashboard exists, demand looks healthy, and nobody can explain why GMV has stalled. The diagnostic is to check whether a supply root and a named convergence node exist at all — often they don't, because the template came from a single-sided product.

8. What good looks like

Six months on, Tarazu Bazaar's metric review looked different from most growth dashboards. Two roots sat side by side, each with a named owner — a supply lead in Delhi, a demand lead in Bengaluru — and between them, on the same slide, sat match rate, co-owned by both, reviewed together every Monday. Any proposal to change take rate now required a seller-retention cohort attached before it reached the board. When a regional dip appeared in Indore that the national average had been quietly absorbing, the city-level cut caught it within a week rather than a quarter, because segmentation was built into the tree from the start. Nobody needed persuading that a healthy-looking supply number and a healthy marketplace were the same thing; the tree itself would not let that confusion survive past the first glance.

9. What Meher decided

Meher walked into the Monday board meeting with Table 1 and the tree diagram, not a slide of listing counts. She recommended killing the blanket ₹500-per-listing bonus, redirecting the budget to a ₹150 completion bonus paired with a search-ranking fix, and presenting match rate — not GMV alone — as the headline number the growth team would be judged on that quarter. The arithmetic did the persuading: a 15.3% projected GMV lift at under a quarter of the cost, with a metric that could only rise if buyers actually found what they searched for. The board approved it, with one condition Meher had already planned for: seller retention, cut by cohort, would appear on the same slide every quarter take rate was discussed.

What Meher still needed next was not another tree but the discipline underneath it: a tree shows correlation, not causation, so she would need a controlled experiment to confirm the ranking fix, rather than some coincident change in retailer behaviour, was what actually moved match rate toward 27%. Two questions worth sitting with, whatever product one manages: which node in your tree could be moved by one side alone, at the other's expense, without anyone noticing for a quarter — and if your convergence metric fell ten points tomorrow, whose job is it to find out why?

Metric Trees for Two-Sided Products: The Deeper Treatment

A marketplace can hold idle supply and unmet demand in the same city on the same day. No single-root funnel has a term for that. The two-rooted tree gives it one — and the arithmetic underneath is older and sharper than most product teams realise.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Tuesday, 11 August 2026, Ira Bhagat, head of product at Imarat Works, sat with a purchase request she did not want to approve. Imarat ran a construction-labour exchange out of Pune: contractors posted job-days — one mason, one site, one date — and registered workers accepted them. July's nine-city panel showed 31,500 weekly-active workers offering some 96,000 worker-days a week, 6,200 contractor accounts posting 19,400 job-days, and 11,900 job-days filled. At a ₹780 day wage that was ₹92.8 lakh of weekly gross merchandise value and, at an 8% contractor fee, ₹7.4 lakh of weekly revenue.

The request came from the Nagpur operations head: ₹40.8 lakh for 12,000 further worker registrations at ₹340 each, because fill rate — filled job-days over posted job-days — stood at 61.3%, so nearly four in ten contractor requests went unserved. It is a hard argument to refuse in a room, since the unserved 38.7% is visible and the idle supply is not. Ira's difficulty was that the same panel put supply-side utilisation — filled job-days over offered worker-days — at 12.4%. Imarat carried almost five worker-days for every job-day posted, and buying more of the long side was, she suspected, the most expensive thing ₹40.8 lakh could do.

Eleven days later and 560 kilometres south, Kalyani Sridhar, chief product officer at Gopuram Health Network in Hyderabad, faced the mirror image. Gopuram connected patients across Hyderabad and six tier-2 cities with empanelled specialists for outpatient consultations. August: 3,400 specialists publishing 214,000 slots, 96,000 patient searches, 41,000 bookings, 33,200 consultations attended — slot fill 19.2%, booking rate 42.7%, show-up 81%. At ₹620 a consultation, monthly GMV was ₹2.06 crore against an 11% fee, or ₹22.6 lakh of revenue. Her chief financial officer wanted 15%, adding ₹8.2 lakh a month for no engineering cost. Kalyani's objection was not that the arithmetic was wrong but that it assumed specialists would behave in September exactly as in August, and no node on her dashboard told her whether that held.

2. What the two-rooted tree is, and what it was invented to solve

Define it precisely. A metric tree for a two-sided product decomposes created value into three things: two population roots instrumented independently; one or more convergence nodes measuring the rate at which each population's intent clears against the other; and feedback edges — take rate, ranking concentration, price — running backwards into the roots with a measurable lag. That third element is why the object is not a tree at all. Practitioners say tree and mean a directed graph with a designated root and a few named cycles.

Its shallow ancestry is the DuPont decomposition of return on equity from the 1920s, by way of the late-2000s growth funnels. Its deep ancestry lies elsewhere: the search-and-matching literature of Peter Diamond, Dale Mortensen and Christopher Pissarides, who shared the 2010 Nobel Memorial Prize for it. That literature exists to explain what ordinary supply-and-demand accounting cannot — an economy holding unemployed workers and unfilled vacancies at the same time, persistently. Its central object is the matching function, M = A · Sα · Dβ, where M is matches per period, S and D the stocks of searching supply and demand, A matching efficiency, and α and β elasticities. Its central ratio is market tightness, θ = S / D.

That is the marketplace problem exactly, and what a one-population funnel cannot express: it has no term for supply idling next to demand starving, and at best calls the gap "conversion". The two-rooted tree makes it a measured object with two readings rather than one residual.

Four schools, and the propositions each will and will not sign

The convergence school wants one shared number both sides are judged on. It signs: a team that reviews two roots separately will optimise the easier one. It will not sign that the convergence node may be a ratio — it insists on a count, weekly matched pairs, because a ratio improves when the business shrinks.

The constraint school, descended from the theory of constraints and a decade of investing memos, holds that one side binds at a time. It signs: an early marketplace should instrument its constraint obsessively and the other side barely at all. It will not sign that both roots deserve equal review time, which it calls symmetry theatre.

The contribution-margin school holds that volume trees are a trap. It signs: a match that loses ₹40 is a negative node. It will not sign that GMV belongs at the root.

The local-markets school denies there is such a thing as the marketplace's tree. It signs: there are forty city-by-category trees and their average is an artefact. It will not sign that a national convergence node is a useful management object.

3. Mechanics: what expert practitioners actually compute

The steps usually left implicit are the first and the third.

First, define intent on both sides in the same unit. Most two-sided trees fail here and never recover: sellers on one side and searches on the other yield a ratio whose terms are not commensurable, and every number below inherits the incoherence. Imarat works in job-days on both sides. Gopuram uses slots and search-intents, defensible only because it defines a search-intent as a specialty-city-week request rather than a page view.

Second, compute both convergence ratios and the tightness between them. Fill rate is M/D, the demand side's experience; utilisation is M/S, the supply side's. Under constant returns they move in opposite directions as θ changes — the most under-appreciated fact in marketplace measurement. Imarat's θ is 4.95; Gopuram's about 2.2.

Third — the step almost nobody takes — estimate the matching function from your own panel. Ira's analyst regressed log weekly matches on log offered worker-days and log posted job-days across 126 city-months, with city fixed effects to absorb the fact that Pune and Nashik are different markets. The result: α = 0.31 on supply, β = 0.74 on demand, summing to 1.05. A 10% rise in posted job-days yields 7.4% more filled job-days; a 10% rise in offered worker-days yields 3.1%. The sum says returns to matching are very nearly constant — a small density benefit, not the compounding flywheel the deck claimed. The decision rule follows directly: the marginal rupee belongs on the side with the higher elasticity per rupee of acquisition cost, not the side with the worse-looking ratio.

Table 1. Imarat Works — cost of a 1% gain in weekly matches, by side
StepSupply sideDemand side
Units to move the root by 1%960 worker-days194 job-days
Yield per acquired account1.15 worker-days/wk3.10 job-days/wk
Accounts needed83563

Spend for a 1% root move₹2.84 lakh₹3.02 lakh

Contractors cost fourteen times more to acquire than workers and are still 2.2 times cheaper per unit of marketplace output. The registration budget buys about 4.5% more matches; the same money on contractor acquisition buys about 10%. No narrative about "unserved demand" survives this table, and no team can build it without first estimating the exponents.

Fourth, draw the feedback edges and attach a lag to each. Take rate feeds back negatively into the supply root with a lag of one to three quarters, because suppliers do not re-plan their channel mix weekly. Ranking relevance feeds back into the tail: it raises the convergence ratio while concentrating matches on the best-rated suppliers. At Imarat, six months of ranking work lifted the top decile's share of matches from 34% to 51% while the bottom half saw matches fall 22% and twelve-week retention drop nine points. Relevance is bought with concentration, and concentration is paid for two quarters later in tail churn.

Fifth, give every node — feedback edges included — an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs: an edge with a measured elasticity and no owner is a fact nobody acts on. Sixth, re-cut every node by market before believing it.

4. When the two-rooted tree applies, stated as tests

Three conditions, each testable on a week of data, each applied to both protagonists.

One: both sides face a real choice and can refuse. If one side is dispatched rather than choosing — employees on a roster, a captive fleet — you have a logistics operation wearing marketplace vocabulary, and its supply root is a capacity plan, not a behavioural metric. Imarat's workers pass; they decline roughly 44% of offers. Gopuram partly fails: for the 41% of slot inventory from three hospital chains, the specialist cannot decline a booking, because the chain's administrator publishes the calendar. That inventory belongs in a capacity node, and Kalyani's tree blended the two — why her take-rate question had no answer on her dashboard.

Two: idle supply and unmet demand genuinely coexist in the same city in the same week. Both companies pass emphatically. If everything offered is always taken, the market is price-cleared and a single-root tree with a pricing node is honest.

Three: matching is non-trivial — not every unit of supply can serve every unit of demand. Imarat matches on trade, site and date; Gopuram on specialty, language and slot time. Where any supply serves any demand, as on a commodity exchange, the two-rooted tree misleads, because it implies matching quality is a lever when only price is.

So is the fully managed marketplace, where the platform sets prices and assigns counterparties: there the convergence node measures the algorithm rather than the market, and a rising match rate may mean only that the algorithm has grown willing to assign poor matches.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product. When Imarat added a wage-advance product — workers drawing 60% of an accepted day's wage the same evening — the tree acquired a second convergence node, advance approval rate, trading against the first: approving more advances raises worker liveness and so the supply root, and also raises default losses sitting in contribution margin. The mature handling is two trees joined only at contribution margin per match, with an explicit rule on which owns the worker relationship in a conflict.

Regulated. Gopuram cannot optimise ranking freely: ordering specialists by booking conversion is arguably a clinical recommendation, and India's telemedicine practice guidelines and state clinical-establishment rules make that exposure real rather than theoretical. Counsel capped personalised ranking at a specialty-and-availability sort, so the tree contains a node with an exogenous ceiling. Experts write the ceiling onto the diagram rather than let a team burn a quarter discovering it — likewise for the fee node wherever a regulator or a network such as ONDC constrains what a platform may charge.

Hardware plus software. Ilaka Freight Exchange, a Surat truck load-matching venture, inferred carrier liveness from ₹4,200 telematics units fitted in member trucks. A firmware regression in March 2026 silenced 3,100 devices and the supply root fell 9% in a fortnight with no change in carrier behaviour. The correction was structural: a device-health node upstream of supply liveness, and a rule that no supply metric is reported in a week when fleet uptime is below 97%. A tree instrumented through hardware inherits the hardware's failures as apparent market events.

AI-native. Gyanmitra Learning Exchange, matching students with tutors, added AI tutors alongside human ones in 2025. The blended convergence ratio rose from 38% to 71% in three quarters and was reported as a triumph. It was an artefact: AI supply is unbounded, so its elasticity is near zero and its utilisation meaningless. Underneath the blend, human-tutor utilisation had fallen fourteen points and churn had doubled. Never blend elastic and inelastic supply in one node.

The organisational seam. Imarat's supply organisation sat in Pune and its demand organisation in Bengaluru, on separate quarterly objectives. What companies say they do about the convergence node is co-own it. What works is one of three things: both roots under one general manager; the convergence node as the only shared term in both teams' variable pay; or a weekly liquidity review with a written decision log, so "co-owned" means someone writes down what changes by Friday. Everything else becomes a number that moves without consequence.

6. Eight nuances that separate expertise from competence

The single liquidity number is a category error. Fill rate and utilisation move in opposite directions as tightness changes, so one number conceals which side is served. The tell is a deck reading "marketplace liquidity: 24%, up 2 points" with no denominator named. An expert asks at once which side's view that is, and what happened to the other.

Denominators are the softest part of any tree. Convergence ratios improve far more cheaply by shrinking what counts as intent than by creating matches: collapsing repeat searches into a session, excluding zero-result queries, auto-rejecting requests unlikely to fill. The tell is a ratio that jumps in a week with nothing shipped. The defence is to make the denominator's growth rate a reported node with an owner.

Ratios do not average across markets. This is arithmetic, not judgement, and it is where most national dashboards lie.

Table 2. Imarat Works, fill rate across two cities, May to July 2026
CityMay postedMay fillJul postedJul fill
Pune8,40074.0%6,10071.5%
Nagpur9,60049.0%13,30056.5%
Combined18,00060.7%19,40061.3%

Pune's fill rate fell, Nagpur's rose, and the national rate rose only because volume shifted toward Nagpur — still the worse market. Nationally this reads as improvement; locally it is a deteriorating Pune masked by mix. Whenever numerator and denominator move across segments at different levels, the aggregate can move opposite to every segment. The expert checks that at least one city moved the way the national number claims.

Take rate is a price, and its elasticity is not uniform across supply. Suppliers with alternative channels are several times more price-sensitive, so a rate increase churns disproportionately the supply hardest to replace. The tell is blended supplier retention looking flat while top-decile retention falls — blended retention being the most reassuring and least informative number on most dashboards.

The constraint moves. Imarat's Pune market is demand-constrained in the dry season and supply-constrained through the monsoon, when site work stops and workers leave for the fields. A tree drawn in January and reviewed identically in July answers last season's question. The tell is a node whose review returns the same conclusion four quarters running.

Match rate is not match quality. A filled job-day ending in a dispute, a no-show or a refund is a negative match the convergence node records as a success. Experts define a durable match with a survival window — at Imarat, one both parties confirm at close of day — and track the gap. The tell is convergence rising while repeat rate falls.

Leakage must be measured, not inferred. Two parties who have met once can transact off-platform forever, and the tree records this as churn on both sides rather than the single phenomenon it is. Proxies exist: decay in the transaction rate of matched pairs, off-platform contact attempts, requests that stop after one fulfilment. The tell is strong first-transaction numbers and weak second ones on both sides.

Counts and ratios answer different questions and both belong. A ratio says whether the mechanism works; a count says whether the business exists. A marketplace whose ratio rises while matched pairs fall is dying efficiently. The tell is a team that quotes one from memory and looks up the other.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer marketplaces demand is fast and elastic, supply slow, and the convergence node is best expressed in time — minutes to a filled request — because consumers abandon rather than wait. In B2B and enterprise the relationship inverts: demand is lumpy, contracted and slow, so the demand root belongs in committed volume rather than sessions, and a monthly cadence is accuracy rather than laziness. Gopuram sits awkwardly between. Where physical goods are involved the supply root gains a dimension software lacks — inventory position and its geography — and a listing that cannot be delivered in the promised window is not supply. In AI products the honest difference is narrower than the discourse suggests: the tree is unchanged, but one side may have near-zero elasticity, which breaks blended ratios. Where there is no real difference, say so: the owner-cadence-decision discipline is identical everywhere.

Stage changes emphasis more than structure. Before liquidity is established the constraint school is simply right: instrument the binding side and one convergence ratio, little else. At scale the centre of gravity shifts to the backward edges, because the roots are large enough that composition matters more than count. The transition is handled badly, since it asks the team that won by obsessing over one number to start distrusting it.

8. Three worked cases

Imarat Works: reallocating the ₹40.8 lakh. Ira redirected the budget to contractor acquisition and a scheduling change letting contractors post job-days three days further ahead. Over ten weeks posted job-days rose 18% to 22,900 while offered worker-days stayed flat. The matching function predicted 0.74 × 18% = 13.3% more matches, or 13,480; the realised figure was 13,610, a 14.4% gain. Weekly GMV reached ₹106.2 lakh. Critically, fill rate fell from 61.3% to 59.4%, exactly as the tightness curve predicts when θ drops. Had fill rate been the single north star, the best quarter in the company's history would have been reported as a regression.

Gopuram Health Network: pricing the supply root. Rather than move the fee everywhere, Kalyani ran 15% in three of seven cities for nine weeks against 11% in the rest. Published slots in the test cities fell 11% by week four and 19% by week nine, bookings fell 8%, and revenue per booking rose 36% — an implied supply elasticity to take rate of −0.52. Quarter-one net revenue rose 21%, exactly as the CFO predicted, but GMV trajectory turned negative at −6% and specialists also listed on a national aggregator churned at 3.1 times the rate of those who were not.

Table 3. Gopuram Health Network, nine-week fee test, three cities against four
MeasureControl (11%)Test (15%)
Slots published, week 9 vs week 0+3%−19%

Specialist churn, multi-homing cohort4.2%13.0%

Hastkala Setu: the failure and the recovery. Hastkala Setu, a Jaipur marketplace matching artisan clusters with overseas boutique buyers, chose a single convergence north star in 2024: buyer-request fill rate. The team moved it from 44% to 79% in two quarters and was rewarded for it. The mechanism was almost entirely denominator engineering — requests judged unlikely to fill were auto-rejected at intake and never entered the denominator, the catalogue narrowed to six fast-moving categories, and onboarding outside them stopped. GMV grew 9%, so nothing looked wrong. Meanwhile active clusters fell from 4,800 to 2,600, and when a European chain arrived wanting three categories Hastkala had quietly exited, it could not serve an order worth an estimated ₹14 crore a year.

The recovery took five quarters. The denominator was redefined to include every request received, auto-rejections included, resetting the reported ratio from 79% to 51%. Catalogue breadth served and artisan twelve-month retention became guardrail nodes with a named owner, and some 900 clusters were re-onboarded at a cost of ₹6.4 crore. The instructive part is that the tree was never wrong and the convergence node was a reasonable choice. What failed was that its denominator had no owner — and a metric whose denominator is unowned will be optimised through the denominator every time.

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of late detection

Buying the long side. Early sign: acquisition spend aimed at whichever side has the uglier ratio. Diagnostic: what is our tightness, and what are our two elasticities? Caught late, the cost is a quarter's budget and an idle supply majority that disengages.

Denominator drift. Early sign: a step change in a ratio with nothing shipped behind it. Diagnostic: plot the denominator alone. Caught late, as at Hastkala Setu, the cost is a narrowed business and a painful restatement.

Take rate treated as free money. Early sign: a fee change approved without a supply-cohort readout. Diagnostic: what is our fee elasticity, estimated from a geographic holdout rather than assumed? Caught two or three quarters late, the cost is the departure of multi-homing suppliers.

National averages over heterogeneous markets. Early sign: the aggregate moves where no market moved. Diagnostic: show me this chart for the three largest cities. Caught late, capital goes to the wrong geography for a planning cycle.

Blending incompatible supply. Early sign: a segment with structurally different elasticity folded into one ratio. Diagnostic: does every unit in this denominator face the same constraint? Caught late, a whole supplier class exits unnoticed, as at Gyanmitra.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Count or ratio at the convergence node. The count camp argues that ratios are gameable by shrinking and that matched pairs per week cannot be improved by doing less; its evidence is the pattern of firms whose liquidity ratios improved as they contracted. The ratio camp argues that counts cannot distinguish a marketplace that works from one merely large, and that any count can be bought. The count camp is wrong where denominators are well-governed — an organisational claim, not a measurement one; the ratio camp is wrong where a firm lacks the maturity to own a denominator, which is most firms.

One constraint or a balanced tree. The constraint school's evidence is strong early: marketplaces are rarely constrained on both sides at once, and split attention has killed more of them than mismeasurement. The balance school's evidence is strong at scale: organisations rewarded on one side for years develop a blindness that survives the constraint's migration. What would settle it is data on how often the binding side switches within a planning cycle, and nobody has published it.

Whether take rate belongs in the tree at all. One camp holds that price is an input, not a metric, and placing it in the tree invites teams to move it as though it were a lever. The other holds that a backward edge with a measured elasticity is how a tree earns its keep, and that excluding price hides the mechanism by which financial pressure destroys supply. The exclusion camp is wrong wherever elasticity has been estimated; the inclusion camp is wrong wherever it has not, because an unmeasured edge invites guessing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this draws a tree with two roots and a convergence node and presents it. Someone who has internalised it asks three questions first: in what unit is intent measured on each side, what is the tightness between them, and what are the two elasticities. They quote both convergence ratios reflexively, never one, and treat every improvement in a ratio as a hypothesis about the denominator until proven otherwise. They know which nodes carry an exogenous ceiling, can name the lag on each backward edge, and when the national number moves favourably their first instinct is suspicion of mix.

12. What Ira and Kalyani decided

Ira declined the registration purchase and put the ₹40.8 lakh into contractor acquisition and posting lead time, on the strength of Table 1. She also changed what the company reported: both convergence ratios alongside tightness, matched job-days as a count, and top-decile share as a standing guardrail. Her concession to Nagpur was real — a budget for certifying workers in the two trades where the city's fill rate was genuinely capacity-constrained, a different claim from "we need more workers" and one the local data supported.

Kalyani did not take the fee to 15%. She settled at 13%, tiered so that single-homing specialists stayed at 11%, and moved the three hospital chains out of the supply root into a contracted-capacity node. Net revenue rose less than the CFO's model promised, and the supply base held.

Discussion questions.

1. Imarat's best quarter showed a falling fill rate. What must a board be told in advance for that to be read correctly, and what does it imply about which number belongs on the first slide?

2. Gopuram's corporate-chain inventory cannot refuse a booking. Does it belong in the supply root, a capacity node, or a separate tree — and what breaks under each choice?

3. Hastkala Setu's convergence node was defensible and still produced a narrower business. Was the failure in the metric, the ownership, or the incentive — and which would you fix first?

13. Going deeper

Metric trees and driver models — the single-root form this page extends; a two-rooted graph built on a sloppy one inherits every defect twice.

Marketplace metrics — the vocabulary that fills the nodes, and what lets you read a rival's disclosures.

What makes a good metric — sensitivity, timeliness, resistance to gaming: the test every node must pass.

Vanity versus actionable metrics — how nodes like registered supplier count get caught early.

The GAME framework — the owner-cadence-decision attachment that turns a diagram into a management system.

Acquisition, retention and monetisation actions — the lever inventory beneath each root, and why elasticity per rupee decides allocation.

Direct versus proxy, magnitude versus ratio — the formal treatment of section 10's count-or-ratio dispute.

North star metric — why two-sided products strain the convention, and the alternatives when one number cannot carry both sides.

Mehfil Events: pricing a wedding marketplace before the season

Aparna Deshmukh has nine days to recommend a commission for the biggest wedding season of Mehfil's life — and two dashboards that disagree about what the last one cost.

1. Nine days before the season

On the evening of 21 November 2026, Aparna Deshmukh sat in Mehfil Events' office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru with two printed dashboards in front of her and a calendar that would not move. On 30 November the company's leadership had to lock its commission structure for the December–February wedding season, the three months in which Mehfil earned close to half of its annual revenue. Harish Nair, the chief executive, had proposed raising the platform commission from 9 per cent to 13 per cent on all vendor bookings. The arithmetic on his slide was one line long: 4,300 bookings a month at an average of ₹1.32 lakh, four extra points of commission, ₹2.27 crore a month.

Aparna did not think the slide was wrong. She thought it was incomplete in a way she could now, for the first time, demonstrate. Six weeks earlier Priya Varadarajan, the company's data scientist in Toronto, had rebuilt Mehfil's reporting as a metric tree with two roots — one descending from bookings into the couples who ask, one descending from bookings into the vendors who answer. The tree made visible a number that Harish's slide treated as a constant and that the July pilot suggested was not.

2. Company background

Mehfil Events, founded in 2019, is a marketplace for wedding services. A couple — more often, in practice, the couple's parents — creates a requirement: a Marwari wedding in Jaipur in February, 600 guests, photography and cinematography, decor, and a makeup artist for three functions. Mehfil surfaces verified vendors, carries the conversation, holds the advance in escrow through a licensed payment aggregator, generates GST-compliant invoices, and releases funds against milestones. It charges the vendor a commission on the booking value; couples pay nothing.

By October 2026 Mehfil had 11,500 vendors transacting in a month across twenty-four cities, from the destination-wedding cluster of Udaipur and Jaipur to the Tamil temple-wedding market around Madurai and Coimbatore. It competes for couples' attention with WedMeGood and ShaadiSaga, with Instagram, where most photographers' portfolios actually live, and with the oldest competitor of all: the family friend who knows a decorator. It competes for vendors with nothing in particular — a good Udaipur photographer is listed everywhere and answers whoever brings work.

The team is spread wide. Engineering sits in Bengaluru and Pune; Daniel Oesterle, the design lead, works from Berlin and joins calls at what is breakfast for him and evening for Bengaluru; Priya is in Toronto; Sharanya Rao runs customer success from Singapore, covering the South-East Asian diaspora; and Vikram Anand sells from Edison, New Jersey, to Indian-American families planning weddings back home. Mehfil's single largest account is Firdaus Weddings, a Dubai planner that books forty to sixty destination weddings a year in Rajasthan and Goa and settles in dirhams.

3. The situation

Mehfil's trouble is not growth. Enquiries have compounded for eleven quarters. Its trouble is that the number Harish reports to investors — gross bookings — and the number Ritu Bhandari worries about in Jaipur — how many good vendors still bother to reply — have started moving in opposite directions, and until October nobody could show that they were connected.

Priya's tree, Exhibit 1, made the connection arithmetic. October's 4,300 paid bookings can be counted down the couples' side — 28,000 active couples, 4.5 enquiries each, 61 per cent answered with a quote inside a day, 5.6 per cent of those quotes converting to a paid booking — or down the vendors' side, as 11,500 active vendors sending 6.7 quotes each and winning 5.6 per cent of them. Both paths land on the same figure, which is the point: whatever Mehfil does to one side has to show up as a number on the other.

The tree also carries a node Harish's slide does not: leakage. Priya estimates from the pattern of conversations that stop abruptly after a phone number is exchanged that roughly 31 per cent of serious couple–vendor pairs settle off the platform on WhatsApp and UPI. That is about 1,900 bookings a month Mehfil helped create and did not earn on.

4. The people

Harish Nair, chief executive, Mumbai. He is nine months from a Series B extension and has told investors Mehfil will exit March 2027 at an annualised ₹85 crore of net revenue. At 9 per cent, the season does not reach that. He is not indifferent to vendors; he believes that in a market where Mehfil brings the work, a good photographer will absorb four points rather than lose the booking.

Ritu Bhandari, head of vendor network, Jaipur. She spends her weeks with decorators and photographers in Udaipur, Jodhpur and Jaipur, the highest-value cluster in the country. She points out that her best vendors already treat Mehfil as one of four sources of work, that they clear 18–22 per cent margins after crew and equipment, and that four points of commission is a fifth of that margin. Her fear is not a protest; it is silence — vendors who stay listed and stop replying.

Priya Varadarajan, data scientist, Toronto. She built the tree and is careful about what it can and cannot prove. She will defend the identity arithmetic in the middle of the tree and will not defend the leakage estimate to better than plus or minus eight points.

Vikram Anand, head of diaspora sales, Edison, New Jersey. His families book from abroad, spend 2.4 times the Indian average, and care about escrow and documentation more than anyone; they will not settle a ₹9 lakh decor booking over UPI from New Jersey. He wants nothing that pushes vendors off the platform, because off-platform settlement is precisely what his clients refuse.

5. The evidence from July

In July 2026 Mehfil ran a three-month commission pilot in Indore and Coimbatore, raising the rate to 13 per cent while twenty-two other cities stayed at 9. Exhibit 2 compares the pilot cities with a matched pair of control cities, Nagpur and Mysuru. It is the only direct evidence in the company about what the extra four points cost.

The pilot's last line is the one that matters and the one most easily misread. Revenue per city rose ₹2 lakh a month — five per cent — while the control cities rose ₹2 lakh on their own. Read through the tree, the mechanism is legible: the extra commission multiplied a smaller number, because two supply leaves — active vendors and quotes per vendor — fell, and because more of what remained moved off the platform altogether.

The two liquidity numbers point in opposite directions across the country. In Udaipur and Jaipur, couples wait — fewer than half of enquiries are answered in a day — while vendors are already sending eleven quotes a month and have more work than they can take. In the tier-2 northern cities, couples are answered promptly and vendors are hungry. A rate that is a fair price in Kanpur is a tax on a constrained side in Udaipur, in the very cluster where Vikram's diaspora families and Firdaus Weddings in Dubai place the largest bookings of the year.

6. The options

Option A — raise the commission to 13 per cent nationally from 1 December. It is simple, it is communicable to vendors in one message, and if vendor behaviour held it would deliver about ₹2.27 crore a month. Its cost is that the July pilot says behaviour does not hold, that the season is the worst possible moment to lose replying vendors, and that the losses land hardest in the destination cluster, where Mehfil has the most to lose per booking.

Option B — hold the commission at 9 per cent and spend the season attacking leakage. Mehfil would make on-platform settlement worth having: escrow-backed advance protection for the couple, guaranteed three-day payouts for the vendor, GST invoicing and dispute cover, and a commission taper — 9 per cent on a vendor's first four bookings in a season, 6 per cent thereafter. Recovering a third of the estimated 1,900 leaked bookings is worth roughly ₹0.75 crore a month at the current rate and strengthens both roots. The cost is that it is slower, the leakage estimate is soft, and Harish's March number is not reached by it alone.

Option C — cut the commission to 6 per cent and sell vendor visibility. A subscription of ₹4,000–₹12,000 a month for priority placement would shift revenue from the transaction to the supply side's marketing budget, and would grow with vendor count rather than with booking value. The cost is that placement bought rather than earned degrades the couples' experience — the demand root's quality leaf — and that Mehfil would be selling attention in the one cluster where attention is already the scarce good.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, write out the two ways of arriving at 4,300 paid bookings. Which leaves does a commission change touch first, and how long would you expect the effect to take?

2. Exhibit 2 shows pilot revenue per city rising 5 per cent. Why is that a weak argument for Option A? What would you need from the control cities to make it a strong one?

3. Exhibit 3 shows two liquidity measures moving in opposite directions across clusters. What does that imply about a single national commission rate?

4. What would you recommend to Harish on 30 November, and which three numbers would you put on the January review to show whether you were right?

8. A note for the learner

This decision looks like a pricing question and is really a measurement question. A single-rooted tree — revenue equals bookings times value times commission — makes the commission look like a free multiplier, because the only nodes on it belong to the demand side. A two-rooted tree forces the question of where the extra four points come from, and answers it: from the vendors' margin, which shows up two months later as fewer active vendors, fewer quotes each, slower replies, and more settlement moving to WhatsApp. All four of those are nodes on the tree, and all four are visible in Exhibit 2.

A well-reasoned answer will do three things. It will treat commission as an input with a lagged cost rather than as an output multiplier. It will refuse to read national averages, because liquidity clears cluster by cluster and Exhibit 3 shows the constraint sitting on opposite sides in Udaipur and in Kanpur. And it will name, in advance, the counter-metrics that would reveal a mistake in time to reverse it during the season.

One defensible path: hold 9 per cent through the season in the destination cluster, where the vendor side is the binding constraint and the average booking is ₹3.10 lakh, and raise to 11 per cent in the tier-2 clusters where vendors are answering promptly and sending under four quotes a month — a segmented version of Option A, funded by the side that is not scarce. Run Option B's settlement benefits and taper everywhere from 1 December, because they lift both roots and are the only lever that grows revenue without taking anything from either side. Report four numbers weekly to Harish: enquiries answered within 24 hours, quotes per active vendor, on-platform settlement share, and commission revenue. The blended rate lands near 10 per cent rather than 13, which does not reach the March number on its own; the argument to make to the board is that the pilot shows 13 does not reach it either, and costs the supply base as well.
